   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times

   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}

   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution

   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.

   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.

   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975	
   976	
   977	
   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.
  1009		\end{enumerate}
  1010	\end{enumerate}

180	\begin{proof}
   181		We first prove the ``if'' direction: if there exist spaces and functions
   182	  satisfying the conditions in the lemma, the fact that $L$ is an $\ell$-level
   183	  CL function follows from \cref{enu:cl-k-cl,enu:cl-last-ell} of the lemma
   184	  statement.
   185	
   186	  We now prove the ``only if'' direction.
   187	  Given a CL function $L$ on $V$, we construct the $k$-th family of subspaces
   188	  and functions for all $k \in \{1, \ldots, \ell\}$ by induction on the level
   189	  $\ell$.
   190	  First consider the base case $\ell=1$.
   191	  Since $L_{<1} = 0$, we omit the mentioning of the prefix $u \in L_{<1}(V)$.
   192	  Define $L_{\leq 1} = L$, the factor space $V_1 = V$, and the linear map $L_1 =
   193	  L$.
   194	  It is straightforward to verify that the conditions in the lemma hold for
   195	  these choices of linear maps and spaces.
   196	  
   197	  Now, assume that the lemma holds for CL functions of level at most $\ell - 1$,
   198	  and we prove the lemma for $\ell$-level CL functions.
   199	  By definition, an $\ell$-level CL function $L$ can be written as
   200	  \begin{equation*}
   201	  	L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})
   202	  \end{equation*}
   203	  for some linear map $L_1 : V_1 \to V_1$ and a family of $(\ell-1)$-level CL
   204	  functions
   205	  \begin{equation*}
   206	    \bigl \{ L_{>1,\, v} : V_{>1} \to V_{>1} \bigr \}_{\, v \in L_1(V_1)}
   207	  \end{equation*}
   208	  where $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ are complementary register subspaces of $V$.
   209	  Next, using the inductive hypothesis on the $(\ell-1)$-level CL function
   210	  $L_{>1,\, v}$ we get that for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$ and all $k \in \{1, 2,
   211	  \ldots, \ell-1\}$ there exist $k$-th marginal functions $L'_{v,\, \le k}:
   212	  V_{>1} \to V_{>1}$, $k$-th factor spaces $V'_{v,\, k,\, u}$, and $k$-th linear
   213	  maps $L'_{v,\, k,\, u}$ of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix $u \in L'_{v,\,
   214	    <k}(V_{>1})$ such that the conditions of the lemma for $L_{>1,\, v}$ hold.
   215	  
   216	  Define the marginal functions $L_{\le k} : V \to V$, factor spaces
   217	  $V_{k,\, u}$ and linear maps $L_{k,\, u}$ for $L$ as follows.
   218	  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
   219	  \item Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ and the first factor space to be $V_1$;
   220	  \item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$, define
   221	    \begin{equation}
   222	      \label{eq:cl-k-def}
   223	      L_{\le k}: x \mapsto x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}})
   224	      \quad\text{for } x\in V;
   225	    \end{equation}
   226		\item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{< k}(V)$, define
   227	    $V_{k,\, u} = V'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$ and $L_{k,\, u} = L'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$
   228	    where $v = u^{V_1} \in L_{1}(V_{1})$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}} \in L'_{v,< k-1}(V_{> 1})$.
   229	  \end{enumerate}
   230	  We verify that the conditions of the lemma are satisfied.
   231	  Since $L'_{v,\, < k}$ is by assumption a $(k-1)$-level CL function on $V_{>
   232	    1}$, we get that $L_{\leq k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$ from
   233	  \cref{eq:cl-k-def}, establishing \cref{enu:cl-k-cl}.
   234	  By the induction hypothesis, we have for all $v\in L_1(V_1)$ and $y \in
   235	  V_{>1}$,
   236	  \begin{equation}
   237	    \label{eq:cl-k-1}
   238	    V_{>1} = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   239	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, y^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}},
   240	  \end{equation}
   241	  which implies that for all $x \in V$ and $v = x^{L_1}$,
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    V = V_1 \oplus \Big ( \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   244	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, x^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}} \Big)
   245	    = V_1 \oplus \Big (\bigoplus_{i=2}^{\ell} V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}} \Big)
   246	    = \bigoplus_{i=1}^\ell V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}}\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  The first equality follows from \cref{eq:cl-k-1} while the second and third
   249	  equalities follow from the definition of $V_{k,\, u}$.
   250	  This establishes \cref{enu:cl-space-sum}.
   251	
   252	  Next, we have that for all $x \in V$, $v = x^{L_1}$, and $k \in
   253	  \{1,2,\ldots,\ell\}$,
   254	  \begin{align}
   255	    \label{eq:cl-last-ell}
   256	    L_{\leq k}(x)
   257	    & = v + L'_{v,\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}}) \\
   258	    & = v + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} x^{L'_{v,\, i}}
   259	    = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} x^{L_{i}}, \label{eq:cl-last-ell2}
   260	  \end{align}
   261	  where $L'_{v,\, i}$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix
   262	  $L'_{v,\, <i}(x)$ and $L_i$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix
   263	  $L_{<i}(x)$.
   264	  The second equality follows from the inductive hypothesis applied to $L'_{v,\,
   265	    <k}$ and the third equality follows from the definition of $L_{i}$.
   266	  Line~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell2} implies \cref{enu:cl-map-sum} of the lemma.
   267	  
   268	  Finally, \Cref{enu:cl-last-ell} follows from~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell} where we
   269	  set $k = \ell$ and observe that $L'_{x^{L_1},\, \le \ell-1}$ is equal to
   270	  $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ by the inductive hypothesis.
   271	  This shows that $L_{\le k}$, $V_{k,\, u}$, and $L_{k,\, u}$ satisfy the
   272	  conditions of the lemma and completes the induction.
   273	\end{proof}
   274	
   275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   327	\end{lemma}
   328	
   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}

   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.

   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,

   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree).

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
   532	
   533	\begin{figure}[ht!]
   534		\begin{center}
   535	    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
   536			\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
   537				\hline
   538				$x_1$ & $x_2$ & $x_3$ \\
   539				\hline 
   540				$x_4$ & $x_5$ & $x_6$ \\	
   541				\hline
   542				$x_7$ & $x_8$ & $x_9$ \\
   543				\hline
   544			\end{tabular}
   545			\caption{The Magic Square game}
   546			\label{fig:ms}
   547			\end{center}
   548	\end{figure}
   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.

   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622

+import Mathlib
+import MIPStarRE.LDT.Basic.ParametersBase
+
+/-!
+# Finite-field bases and the fixed binary representation
+
+The Pauli basis test uses fields of size `2^k` for odd `k`, together with a
+chosen self-dual normal basis over `ZMod 2`.  This file records that choice as
+data, while exposing Mathlib's basis and algebra-trace APIs for later proofs.
+
+## References
+
+The declarations correspond to `def:admissible-size`, `def:subfields-kappa`,
+`def:subfield-trace`, and `def:binary-representation` in
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-232` and `298-315`.
+Their paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502,653-728`.
+-/
+
+open scoped BigOperators
+
+namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
+
+/-- `IsAdmissibleSize q` is the predicate `q = 2^k` for an odd exponent.
+This is `def:admissible-size` in the blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:210-212`, with paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:662-667`.
+-/
+def IsAdmissibleSize (q : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ q = 2 ^ k
+
+/--
+A fixed finite-field model records the carrier and the chosen coding of its
+elements by `Fin q`.  The algebra structure and stored basis data make explicit
+the paper's once-and-for-all self-dual normal-basis convention; they are
+deliberately part of the model rather than quantified afresh by the soundness
+theorem.  This is the Lean carrier for `def:binary-representation`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-728`.
+-/
+/- The finite-field carrier is specialized to `Type 0`, as are the finite
+models used by the surrounding Euclidean-space API. -/
+structure FixedFieldModel (q : ℕ) extends MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel.{0} q where
+  /-- Scalar restriction from `ZMod 2` to the chosen field. -/
+  algebra : Algebra (ZMod 2) K
+  /-- Dimension of the chosen basis over the prime subfield. -/
+  basisDim : ℕ
+  /-- The chosen basis dimension is odd, as required for a self-dual normal basis
+  over the binary field. -/
+  basisDimOdd : Odd basisDim
+  /-- The admissible field-size relation for the chosen basis dimension. -/
+  basisCard : q = 2 ^ basisDim
+  /-- The chosen basis of `K` over `ZMod 2`. -/
+  basis : Module.Basis (Fin basisDim) (ZMod 2) K
+  /--
+  The inherited coding of `K` is the natural binary encoding of the stored
+  basis coordinates.  This field records the source's `downsize` convention
+  rather than allowing an unrelated permutation of `Fin q`.  It is the
+  coordinate clause of `def:binary-representation` in
+  `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, with paper origin
+  `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:669-680`.
+  -/
+  representation_natural :
+    ∀ v : Fin basisDim → ZMod 2,
+      (toFieldModel.equiv (basis.equivFun.symm v)).val =
+        ∑ i : Fin basisDim, if v i = 1 then 2 ^ i.1 else 0
+  /-- Self-duality of the chosen basis with respect to the field trace. -/
+  selfDual : ∀ i j, Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (basis i * basis j) =
+    if i = j then 1 else 0
+  /-- Normality of the chosen basis, recorded by a Frobenius generator. -/
+  normal : ∃ α : K, ∀ i, basis i = α ^ (2 ^ i.1)
+
+/-!
+The paper fixes the field representation and self-dual normal basis once for
+each admissible field size.  We expose that choice through a single global
+selector rather than carrying a potentially different model in every game
+parameter record.  Existence is a named stage-4.3 proof obligation; the
+selector itself is the resulting noncomputable choice.
+-/
+
+/-- An admissible binary field size admits the fixed self-dual normal model used
+by the Pauli basis test.  This is the existence assertion implicit in
+`def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis` and `def:binary-representation`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:277-315`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`.

+The construction of the basis and its natural coding is deferred to the
+algebra stage; keeping it as a named theorem makes the proof obligation visible
+without adding a model hypothesis to the source-facing test statements.
+-/
+theorem exists_fixed_field_model (q : ℕ) (hq : IsAdmissibleSize q) :
+    Nonempty (FixedFieldModel q) := by
+  sorry

+/-- The once-and-for-all field model selected for an admissible size.  Every
+QPBT parameter record uses this same choice, matching the paper's fixed
+self-dual normal-basis identification rather than quantifying over arbitrary
+representations.  Blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`; paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`.

+    FixedFieldModel q :=

+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Field F.K := F.toFieldModel.instField
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Fintype F.K := F.toFieldModel.instFintype
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : DecidableEq F.K := F.toFieldModel.instDecidableEq
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Algebra (ZMod 2) F.K := F.algebra
+
+/-- The fixed binary representation of field elements (`def:binary-representation`).
+Blueprint: `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`; paper origin:
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`.
+-/
+noncomputable def binaryEquiv {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K ≃ Fin q :=
+  F.toFieldModel.equiv
+
+/-- The fixed binary representation obtained from the chosen basis coordinates. -/
+noncomputable def binaryRepresentation {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K ≃ Fin q :=
+  binaryEquiv F
+
+/--
+The coordinate map associated with a finite basis.  This is the `κ` of
+`def:subfields-kappa` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-208`,
+whose paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502`.
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev kappa {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F] [Semiring K]
+    [Algebra F K] [Finite ι]
+    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K ≃ₗ[F] (ι → F) :=

+/--
+Multiplication by `a` in basis coordinates, using Mathlib's
+`Algebra.leftMulMatrix`.  It is the multiplication table `K_a` in
+`def:subfields-kappa` (blueprint lines 196-199; paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev multiplicationTable {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F]
+    [Semiring K] [Algebra F K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K →ₐ[F] Matrix ι ι F :=
+  Algebra.leftMulMatrix b

+/--
+The finite-field trace used by the Pauli phases.  This is a thin wrapper around
+Mathlib's basis-independent `Algebra.trace`, matching `def:subfield-trace` and
+Equation `eq:def-trace` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`
+(`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev binTrace (K : Type*) [CommRing K] [Algebra (ZMod 2) K] :
+    K →ₗ[ZMod 2] ZMod 2 :=
+  Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K
+
+/-- The trace selected by a fixed model; this is the map denoted `tr` in the
+paper's `def:binary-representation`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`. -/
+noncomputable def fixedBinTrace {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K → ZMod 2 :=
+  binTrace F.K
+
+/--
+The matrix-trace presentation of `fixedBinTrace`, a statement-level bridge to
+Equation `eq:def-trace`.  It is the trace assertion in `def:subfield-trace`,
+blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`.  It remains a proof
+obligation in stage 4.1.
+-/
+theorem fixedBinTrace_eq_matrixTrace {q ι : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q)
+    (b : Module.Basis (Fin ι) (ZMod 2) F.K) (a : F.K) :
+    fixedBinTrace F a = (multiplicationTable b a).trace := by
+  sorry
+
+end MIPStarRE.QPBT

## (d) Statement sketch of `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`

```lean
/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))

/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
theorem pauli_soundness :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
            ∀ W : PauliKind,
              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
                ‖(heteroKron
                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
              (symmetric B-side bound)
```

   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}

   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}

   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   241		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   242		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   243		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   244		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   245		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   246	\end{definition}

   248	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   249		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   250			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   251		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   252		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   253		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   254		\begin{enumerate}
   255			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   257			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   258			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   260			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   261			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   262		\end{enumerate}
   263		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	\begin{proof}
   266		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   267		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   268		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   269		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   270		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   271		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   272		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   273		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   274		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   275	\end{proof}

   277	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   278		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   279		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   280		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   281		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   282		vector in $\F_2^k$.

   285		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$

   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.

   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}

   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}
   652	
   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.

    26	/--
    27	`registerSubmodule K S` is the span of the standard coordinate vectors indexed

    29	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:24-29`, whose paper origin is
    30	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-239`.

    32	def registerSubmodule (K : Type*) [Field K] (S : Finset ι) : Submodule K (ι → K) :=
    33	  Submodule.span K {v | ∃ i, i ∈ S ∧ v = Pi.single i 1}
    34	
    35	/--
    36	`dotOrthogonal W` consists of vectors whose coordinate dot product with every
    37	member of `W` vanishes.  This is `def:dot-product-orthogonal` in
    38	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:31-42`, with paper origin
    39	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:241-255`.
    40	-/
    41	def dotOrthogonal (W : Submodule K (ι → K)) : Submodule K (ι → K) where
    42	  carrier := {u | ∀ v, v ∈ W → dotProduct u v = 0}
    43	  zero_mem' := by
    44	    intro v hv
    45	    simp [dotProduct]
    46	  add_mem' := by
    47	    intro u v hu hv w hw
    48	    calc
    49	      dotProduct (u + v) w =
    50	          (dotProduct u w) + (dotProduct v w) := by
    51	            change (∑ i, (u i + v i) * w i) =
    52	              (∑ i, u i * w i) + (∑ i, v i * w i)
    53	            simp_rw [add_mul]
    54	            rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    55	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu w hw, hv w hw, add_zero]
    56	  smul_mem' := by
    57	    intro c u hu v hv
    58	    calc
    59	      dotProduct (c • u) v = c * dotProduct u v := by
    60	        simp [dotProduct, smul_eq_mul, mul_assoc, Finset.mul_sum]
    61	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu v hv, mul_zero]

    63	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to the first `k` coordinates.  Lean-only rank
    64	infrastructure for `def:canonical-complement`, blueprint
    65	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`, paper `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    66	-/
    67	private def prefixMap (k n : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    68	    (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin k → K) :=
    69	  { toFun := fun x i => x ⟨i.1, lt_of_lt_of_le i.2 hk⟩
    70	    map_add' := by
    71	      intro x y
    72	      rfl
    73	    map_smul' := by
    74	      intro c x
    75	      rfl }
    76	
    77	/-- The rank of a prefix restriction used by the pivot characterization. -/
    78	private noncomputable def prefixRank {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
    79	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) : ℕ :=
    80	  Module.finrank K (W.map (prefixMap k n hk))
    81	
    82	/--
    83	The non-pivot coordinate set of `W`, defined by the rank-increase
    84	characterization of pivots.  This is the basis-free encoding approved for
    85	`def:canonical-complement` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`;
    86	the paper's Gaussian-elimination presentation is
    87	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`.
    88	-/
    89	noncomputable def canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
    90	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : Finset (Fin n) :=
    91	  Finset.univ.filter fun j =>
    92	    prefixRank W (j.1 + 1) (Nat.succ_le_of_lt j.2) =
    93	      prefixRank W j.1 j.2.le
    94	
    95	/--
    96	The canonical coordinate complement spans a complement of `W`.  This is the
    97	proposition `lem:canonical-complement` in
    98	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:112-120`, with paper origin
    99	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:342-373`.
   100	The proof is intentionally deferred in the stage-4.1 skeleton.
   101	-/
   102	theorem isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
   103	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) :
   104	    IsCompl W (registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)) := by
   105	  sorry
   106	
   107	/--
   108	The projector onto the canonical coordinate complement along `W`.  This is
   109	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:133-145`,
   110	originating at `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:375-384`.
   111	-/
   112	noncomputable def canonicalProjOfKernel {n : ℕ}
   113	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin n → K) := by
   114	  let T := registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)
   115	  let p : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] T :=
   116	    Submodule.projectionOnto T W
   117	      (isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement W).symm
   118	  exact T.subtype.comp p
   119	
   120	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     4	/-!
     5	# Lines and canonical representatives
     6	
     7	The classical and Pauli question distributions use affine lines in a finite
     8	coordinate space.  This module keeps the zero-direction case explicit and
     9	provides the canonical projection used for line representatives.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The source-facing nodes are `def:line`, `prop:line-equiv`, and
    14	`def:line-representative` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:433-492`.
    15	The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:102-174`.
    16	-/
    17	
    18	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    19	
    20	open scoped BigOperators
    21	
    22	variable {K : Type*} [Field K]
    23	
    24	/--
    25	The affine line through `u` in direction `v`, including the singleton case
    26	`v = 0`.  Blueprint `def:line`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:439-453`;
    27	paper origin
    28	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-124`.
    29	-/
    30	def linePoints {m : ℕ}
    31	    (u v : Fin m → K) : Set (Fin m → K) :=
    32	  {x | ∃ t : K, x = u + t • v}
    33	
    34	/-- The elementary coordinate direction used in the axis-parallel predicate of
    35	`def:line`; blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:439-453`, paper origin
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-124`.
    37	-/
    38	def coordinateDirection {m : ℕ}
    39	    (i : Fin m) : Fin m → K :=
    40	  Pi.single i 1
    41	
    42	/--
    43	`IsAxisParallel v` means that `v` is a standard coordinate direction.  This is
    44	the axis-parallel clause of `def:line` (blueprint lines 445-450; paper
    45	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-124`).
    46	-/
    47	def IsAxisParallel {m : ℕ} (v : Fin m → K) : Prop :=
    48	  ∃ i : Fin m, v = coordinateDirection i
    49	
    50	/--
    51	The diagonal-direction predicate from `def:line`; a prefix of coordinates may
    52	vanish.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:439-453`; paper origin
    53	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-124`.
    54	-/
    55	def IsDiagonal {m : ℕ} (v : Fin m → K) : Prop :=
    56	  ∃ i : Fin m, ∀ j : Fin m, j.1 < i.1 → v j = 0
    57	
    58	/--
    59	Changing the base point to another point on a line leaves the line unchanged.
    60	This is `prop:line-equiv` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:455-466`,
    61	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:128-132`.
    62	-/
    63	theorem linePoints_eq_of_mem {m : ℕ}
    64	    (u v u' : Fin m → K) (h : u' ∈ linePoints u v) :
    65	    linePoints u v = linePoints u' v := by
    66	  sorry
    67	
    68	/--
    69	The canonical linear representative map of a line direction.  It projects onto
    70	the coordinate complement of the span of `v`; for `v = 0` the span is bottom,
    71	so the resulting map is the identity.  Blueprint `def:line-representative`,
    72	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:472-492`; paper origin
    73	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:143-174`.
    74	-/
    75	noncomputable def lineRepMap {m : ℕ}
    76	    (v : Fin m → K) : (Fin m → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin m → K) :=
    77	  canonicalProjOfKernel (Submodule.span K ({v} : Set (Fin m → K)))
    78	
    79	/- The point-valued companion to `lineRepMap`; Lean-only notation for the
    80	canonical representative in `def:line-representative`. -/
    81	/-- The canonical representative point `lineRepMap v u`.  Blueprint
    82	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:472-492`, paper origin
    83	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:166-174`.
    84	-/
    85	noncomputable def lineRep {m : ℕ}
    86	    (u v : Fin m → K) : Fin m → K :=
    87	  lineRepMap v u
    88	
    89	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     4	/-!
     5	# The low-degree encoding
     6	
     7	This module encodes the Boolean subcube by multilinear indicator polynomials
     8	and packages the resulting low-degree code as honest polynomial representatives.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	The source-facing nodes are `def:polynomials-degree`,
    13	`def:low-degree-encoding`, and `def:indicator-vector` in
    14	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:321-417`; the paper origin is
    15	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    16	The polynomial class `def:polyfunc` is reused from
    17	`MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` (the LDT formalization).
    18	-/
    19	
    20	open scoped BigOperators
    21	open MvPolynomial
    22	
    23	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    24	
    25	/- The Boolean cube indexes the `2^m` qudits in the low-degree encoding. -/
    26	/-- The Boolean cube indexing the `2^m` qudits of the test.  This is the index
    27	type in `def:low-degree-encoding`, blueprint
    28	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`, paper origin
    29	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    30	-/
    31	abbrev Cube (m : ℕ) := Fin m → Bool
    32	
    33	/--
    34	The representative polynomial which is `1` at `y` on the Boolean cube and
    35	zero at the other cube points.  This is the indicator polynomial in
    36	`def:low-degree-encoding` (blueprint lines 381-401; paper
    37	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`).
    38	-/
    39	noncomputable def indicatorPoly {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ} (y : Cube m) :
    40	    MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    41	  ∏ i : Fin m, if y i then X i else (1 - X i)
    42	
    43	/--
    44	The multilinear low-degree encoding of a coefficient string.  Polynomial
    45	representatives are used, as fixed by issue #0004, rather than quotienting by
    46	functional equality.  Blueprint: `def:low-degree-encoding`,
    47	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`; paper origin:
    48	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    49	-/
    50	noncomputable def lowDegreeEncoding {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    51	    (a : Cube m → K) : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K :=
    52	  ∑ y : Cube m, a y • indicatorPoly y
    53	
    54	/- Evaluation shorthand for the representative polynomial in
    55	`def:low-degree-encoding`; it is Lean-only notation. -/
    56	/-- Evaluation shorthand for the low-degree encoding.  Blueprint
    57	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:381-401`, paper origin
    58	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    59	-/
    60	noncomputable def lowDegreeEnc {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    61	    (a : Cube m → K) (x : Fin m → K) : K :=
    62	  eval x (lowDegreeEncoding a)
    63	
    64	/--
    65	The indicator vector `ind_m(x)` of `def:indicator-vector`.
    66	Blueprint: `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:403-417`; paper origin:
    67	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    68	-/
    69	noncomputable def indicatorVec {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    70	    (x : Fin m → K) : Cube m → K :=
    71	  fun y => eval x (indicatorPoly y)
    72	
    73	/--
    74	The defining dot-product identity for the encoding, corresponding to
    75	Equation `eq:low-degree-encoding-definition` and `lem:indicator-vector` in the
    76	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:403-417`, paper origin
    77	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:832-897`.
    78	It is a proof obligation in stage 4.1.
    79	-/
    80	theorem lowDegreeEnc_eq_dotProduct {K : Type*} [CommRing K] {m : ℕ}
    81	    (a : Cube m → K) (x : Fin m → K) :
    82	    lowDegreeEnc a x = dotProduct a (indicatorVec x) := by
    83	  sorry
    84	
    85	/-- Re-export of the LDT polynomial representative class (`def:polyfunc`).
    86	Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:321-329`; paper origin
    87	`references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex:89-119`.
    88	-/
    89	noncomputable abbrev polyFunc (m d : ℕ) (K : Type*) [CommSemiring K] :
    90	    Submodule K (MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) :=
    91	  MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc m K d
    92	
    93	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     5	/-!
     6	# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states
     7	
     8	The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
     9	are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
    10	operator algebra.  The Fourier/orthogonality identities are retained as named
    11	proof obligations for subsequent stages.
    12	
    13	## References
    14	
    15	The source-facing nodes are `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`, `def:generalized-pauli`,
    16	and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion` in
    17	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:494-652`.  The paper origin is
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.
    19	-/
    20	
    21	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    22	
    23	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    24	
    25	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    26	
    27	variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
    28	  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]
    29	
    30	/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in `def:generalized-pauli`,
    31	blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    32	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    33	-/
    34	inductive PauliKind where
    35	  | X
    36	  | Z
    37	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    38	
    39	/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
    40	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.
    41	
    42	It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
    43	character in their statement types. -/
    44	noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
    45	  if t = 0 then 1 else -1
    46	
    47	/--
    48	The shift operator `τ^X(a)`.  Blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`,
    49	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`; paper origin
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    51	-/
    52	noncomputable def tauShift (a : K) : Op K :=
    53	  fun i j => if i = j + a then 1 else 0
    54	
    55	/--
    56	The phase operator `τ^Z(b)`, with the fixed binary trace in the phase.  It is
    57	the second operator of `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 529-571; paper
    58	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`).
    59	-/
    60	noncomputable def tauPhase (b : K) : Op K :=
    61	  fun i j => if i = j then phaseSign (binTrace K (b * j)) else 0
    62	
    63	/-- The single-qudit eigenvector coordinate used in the tensor-product basis;
    64	see `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1126-1161`. -/
    65	private noncomputable def singlePauliVec (W : PauliKind) (e x : K) : ℂ :=
    66	  match W with
    67	  | .Z => if x = e then 1 else 0
    68	  | .X =>
    69	      (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * phaseSign (binTrace K (e * x))
    70	
    71	/--
    72	The normalized single/multi-qudit eigenvector for a Pauli basis label.  For an
    73	index type `ι`, the input `e : ι → K` labels the tensor-product basis vector.
    74	This is the vector form of `def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint
    75	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:550-570`, paper origin
    76	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`.
    77	-/
    78	noncomputable def pauliVec {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    79	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) (x : ι → K) : ℂ :=
    80	  ∏ i : ι, singlePauliVec W (e i) (x i)
    81	
    82	/--
    83	The rank-one projector onto `pauliVec W e`.  This is the projective measurement
    84	element `τ^W_e` in `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 562-570; paper
    85	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`).
    86	-/
    87	noncomputable def pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    88	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    89	  Matrix.vecMulVec (pauliVec W e) (fun x => star (pauliVec W e x))
    90	
    91	/-- A compact operator-valued form of a generalized Pauli observable from
    92	`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    93	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    94	-/
    95	noncomputable def tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    96	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    97	  fun x y =>
    98	    ∏ i : ι,
    99	      match W with
   100	      | .X => tauShift (a i) (x i) (y i)
   101	      | .Z => tauPhase (a i) (x i) (y i)
   102	
   103	/--
   104	The EPR vector on a finite label space.  Blueprint `def:EPR`,
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
   107	-/
   108	noncomputable def eprState (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   109	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (V × V) :=
   110	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (V × V) ℂ).symm
   111	    (fun p : V × V =>
   112	      if p.1 = p.2 then (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ else 0)
   113	
   114	/-- The EPR vector is normalized on a nonempty finite carrier; see
   115	`def:EPR`, `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`. -/
   116	theorem eprState_norm (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   117	    ‖eprState V‖ = 1 := by
   118	  sorry
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in the Pauli projectors.
   122	This is `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, equations `eq:pauli-obs-proj` and
   123	`eq:pauli-inversion-0`, in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`;
   124	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   125	Both directions are deliberately left as proof-level obligations in stage 4.1.
   126	-/
   127	theorem tauObservable_eq_sum_pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   128	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) :
   129	    tauObservable W a =
   130	      ∑ e : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • pauliProj W e := by
   131	  sorry
   132	
   133	/-- The inverse Fourier expansion of a Pauli projector
   134	(`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`), blueprint
   135	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`, paper origin
   136	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   137	-/
   138	theorem pauliProj_eq_avg_tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   139	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) :
   140	    pauliProj W e =
   141	      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
   142	        ∑ a : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • tauObservable W a := by
   143	  sorry
   144	
   145	end MIPStarRE.QPBT
